summary: This RFC specifies an application-layer protocol for Real-time Inter-network Defense (RID) that passes RID messages over HTTP with TLS. RID messages extend the IODEF XML format used for sharing incident information.

plainLanguage.summary: RID lets security teams send each other messages about incidents. This document says how to send those messages over a web-style connection protected by TLS, and how a reply can come back later on a separate connection. It also sets the rules for the certificates each side presents, so both can be sure who they are talking to.

questions: how are rid messages sent over http
what is the rid callback token
subtitle: How security teams send incident messages to each other over HTTP protected by TLS.

tldr.problem: Real-time Inter-network Defense needs a protocol, not just a message format, so that the security teams in a consortium can interoperate. The RID message format alone does not say how messages travel.
tldr.mechanism: The document carries RID messages inside HTTP requests and responses over TLS. Every RID system acts as both an HTTP client and an HTTP server, posts messages to the root path with a text/xml content type, and can accept a later reply through a callback with its own token.
tldr.outcome: This document replaced RFC 6046, raised the minimum TLS version to 1.1 with 1.2 recommended, and added the RID-Callback-Token header. IANA assigned port 4590/tcp to RID over HTTP/TLS.

today: RFC 6546 is a Proposed Standard. It replaced RFC 6046, which it moves to Historic status. The metadata for this RFC lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What RID Transport Does
sections.content:
The Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF) of RFC 5070 describes an XML document format for exchanging data between Computer Security Incident Response Teams, or those responsible for security incident handling for service providers. The document format gives CSIRTs a simple way to exchange data that can be easily parsed.

IODEF defines a message format, not a protocol. How the messages are shared is left out of scope, so that CSIRTs can exchange and store messages in a way that suits their own incident-handling processes. Real-time Inter-network Defense (RID) of RFC 6545 does require a protocol, to ensure interoperability among the members of a RID consortium. This document specifies the transport of RID messages inside HTTP request and response messages over TLS, that is, over HTTP/TLS. Any IODEF message may also travel this way, by sending it as a RID Report message.
sections.plainLanguage: Security teams need to exchange details of incidents with each other. RID is the format they use for those messages. This document says how the messages travel and who may read them.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 6046
sections.content:
The document lists its changes from its predecessor, RFC 6046:

  • The status of the document is Standards Track.
  • The document is updated to refer to the updated RID specification, RFC 6545, where appropriate.
  • The language about using HTTP/1.1 and TCP ports for RID transport is clarified.
  • The RID-Callback-Token entity header field is added, so that RID replies can be matched during a callback independently of the content of the underlying RID message.
  • The minimum required version of TLS is upgraded to 1.1, and the minimum recommended version to 1.2.
  • The language about a public key infrastructure for RID over HTTPS is clarified and updated to refer to RFC 6125.

This document replaces RFC 6046 and moves it to Historic status.
sections.plainLanguage: This version adds a token that lets a later reply be matched to the original request, and raises the lowest version of TLS that is allowed.

sections.title: Sending a RID Message over HTTP/TLS
sections.content:
Each RID server is both an HTTP/TLS server and an HTTP/TLS client. When a RID message is sent, the sending RID system connects to the receiving RID system, sends the message, and optionally receives a message in reply. Every RID system must be prepared to accept HTTP/TLS connections from any RID peer it communicates with, so that a callback for a delayed reply can reach it.

BCP 56 of RFC 3205 lists the considerations when HTTP is used for an application protocol: the size of the payload for the application, whether a web browser will be used, whether the protocol should be defined on a port other than 80, and whether the security provided by HTTP/TLS suits the application. The document acknowledges that HTTP/TLS is not ideally suited to RID transport, because HTTP is a client-server protocol while RID is a message-exchange protocol, but says the ease of implementation over HTTP/TLS outweighs those concerns. RID systems listen for TCP connections on port 4590, may be configurable to listen on other ports, and should not use TCP port 443, the standard port for HTTP over TLS, so that ordinary HTTP/TLS servers are not mistaken for RID systems.

RID systems must implement all the required functionality of HTTP/1.1. Every RID message sent in an HTTP request must use the POST method with a Request-URI of '/'. As RID documents are XML, the Content-Type request and response headers must be 'text/xml'. The GET and HEAD methods have no particular meaning on a RID system, and a RID system should answer 'GET /' or 'HEAD /' with 204 No Content. Other Request-URIs are reserved for future use, and access to them by any method should return the appropriate HTTP error, 404 Not Found.

Since the content of RID messages is essentially declarative, a RID system interrupted during transport may simply repeat the transaction. Sending a RID message is idempotent.
sections.plainLanguage: Each RID system is both a web server and a web client. To send a message it connects to the other system and posts the message to the root path. Sending the same message twice has the same effect as sending it once, so an interrupted transfer can simply be repeated.

sections.title: The RID Callback Mechanism
sections.content:
The queries and replies in a RID message exchange may be significantly separated in time, so RID over HTTP/TLS supports a callback mechanism. The receiving RID system may return a 202 Accepted response, called a RID callback, instead of a RID message. The callback must contain a zero-length entity body and a 'RID-Callback-Token' entity header field, itself containing a unique token generated by the receiving RID system.

The RID-Callback-Token is an opaque, whitespace-free string of up to 255 printable ASCII characters that must uniquely identify the callback among all callbacks from the receiving RID system to the sending RID system. Because generating a RID Result or Report response may take a long time, there is no upper bound on the time period for that uniqueness requirement. Its ABNF form is callback-token = 1*255(VCHAR).

When performing a callback, the responding system must connect to the host at the network-layer address from which the original request was sent. There is no mechanism in RID for a redirected callback. The callback should use TCP port 4590 unless configured to use a different port.

While a RID system should return the reply in an HTTP response if it is available immediately or within a generally accepted HTTP client timeout of about thirty seconds, this is not mandatory. RID systems must be prepared for a query to be met with a 202 Accepted, an empty response body, a connection termination and a callback. All RID messages require a response from the receiving RID system, so a sending system can expect either an immediate response or a callback.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the answer takes a long time to prepare. The receiving system can then answer straight away with an acceptance and a token, and send the real answer later on a new connection. The token tells the sender which pending request the later answer belongs to.

sections.title: Message Types and Response Codes
sections.content:
The document lists the allowable RID message types in an HTTP response for each RID message type in the request. A RID system must be prepared to handle a response of the given type when it sends the corresponding request, and must not send a response containing any RID message other than the one corresponding to the request it received.

An InvestigationRequest may be answered with an Acknowledgement, a Result or a Report, all with status code 200, or with an empty 202 Accepted. A TraceRequest may be answered the same way. A Query may be answered with an Acknowledgement or a Report, both with status code 200, or with an empty 202. An Acknowledgement, a Result and a Report may each be sent as a callback, and each is answered with status code 200 and an empty response. A Report may also be answered with an Acknowledgement.

If a RID system receives an improper RID message in an HTTP request, it must return an appropriate 4xx Client Error result code to the requesting system. If it cannot process a RID message received in a request because of an error on its own side, it must return an appropriate 5xx Server Error result code. HTTP provides no mechanism for signalling to a server that a response body is not a valid RID message, so a RID system that receives an improper RID message in a response, or cannot process one because of an error on its own side, must log the error and present it to the RID system administrator for handling. The error logging format is an implementation detail and is out of scope for this specification.

RID systems must support and should use HTTP/1.1 persistent connections. They must support chunked transfer encoding on the HTTP server side, so that clients that do not need to pre-calculate message sizes before constructing HTTP headers can be served.
sections.plainLanguage: The document lists which answer each kind of request may get, and which status code carries it. A request can be answered with an acknowledgement, a result or a report, or with an empty acceptance when the answer will follow later.

sections.title: TLS, Certificates and Peer Verification
sections.content:
RID systems must use TLS version 1.1 or higher for confidentiality, identification and authentication when sending RID messages over HTTPS. They must use mutual authentication: both RID systems acting as HTTPS clients and RID systems acting as HTTPS servers must be identified by an X.509 certificate, and mutual authentication requires full path validation on each certificate.

The TLS session must use non-NULL ciphersuites for authentication, integrity and confidentiality. Sessions may be renegotiated within those constraints.

All RID systems should be identified by a certificate containing a DNS-ID identifier as in Section 6.4 of RFC 6125. Including Common Names (CN-IDs) in certificates identifying RID systems is not recommended. RID systems must verify the reference identifiers of their peers against those stored in the certificates presented. Wildcards must not appear in the DNS-ID or CN-ID of a certificate identifying a RID system.

RID systems must support verification of certificates against an explicit whitelist of peer certificates. They should support verification of reference identifiers by matching the DNS-ID or CN-ID with a reverse DNS lookup of the connecting RID peer, and that lookup should be allowed to be cached or done in advance, so that verification still works during instability or compromise of DNS itself.

The use of stable DNS names to address RID systems is recommended. Besides making it easier to connect within a consortium, these names are used as reference identifiers for a RID system's peers. For security purposes, RID systems should not return 3xx Redirection response codes and should not follow any 3xx redirection. The protocol provides no in-band method for handling a change of address of a RID system.

RID systems must support TLS version 1.1 and should support TLS version 1.2. They must not request, offer or use any version of SSL, or any version of TLS prior to 1.1, because of known security vulnerabilities in earlier versions of the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Connections are protected with TLS, and each side presents a certificate so the other can check who it is. Certificates are checked against a list of known peers or against a reverse lookup of the address, and the TLS version must be 1.1 or later.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: In addition to the paragraphs in Section 3 on the use of TLS to secure RID message transport, all the security considerations of related documents apply, especially the Incident Object Description Exchange Format of RFC 5070 and Real-time Inter-network Defense of RFC 6545. The protocol described here is built on the foundation of those documents, and the security considerations they contain are incorporated by reference.
sections.plainLanguage: The security rules of the RID and IODEF documents apply here too, because this document only adds the transport underneath them.
